story.title: DOJ v. California Noncitizen-Ballot Fight Reaches the Ninth Circuit
story.summary: The Justice Department is suing California, alleging the state mailed 2026 ballots to more than 20,000 people it believes are likely noncitizens, and is seeking emergency court orders to have those ballots set aside before they are counted, while California and county officials say DOJ's list is unverified and its demands unlawful.
story.development: On Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, a three-judge Ninth Circuit panel held a rare, nearly two-hour emergency oral argument on DOJ's request for an injunction pending appeal to block roughly 20,000 California mail ballots. Two of the three judges, including a Trump appointee, voiced skepticism about both DOJ's jurisdiction to bring the appeal before the district court ruled and the reliability of its noncitizen list. The panel took the case under submission without ruling, ahead of a separate Oct. 27 hearing before the district judge on DOJ's request for a temporary restraining order.

review.known: DOJ sued California on Oct. 15, alleging the state mailed ballots to more than 20,000 people it believes are likely noncitizens, after a 48-hour review deadline California called unworkable [F8][F9]. Los Angeles County says it never opened DOJ's USB drive of names, citing data-security rules [F10]. On Oct. 19, DOJ charged 28 green-card holders with election-related felonies [F11]. DOJ then pressed counties to segregate suspect ballots and took its fight to the Ninth Circuit after the district judge hadn't ruled; outlets disagree on how many counties were contacted, from at least 18 to 57 of 58 to all of them [F12][F13]. California disputes the list's accuracy, citing a sampled birthplace statistic that itself conflicts across sources, 25.8% versus 38.9% [F14].
review.unknown: It's unknown whether the Ninth Circuit will rule before Judge Carter's Oct. 27 hearing, or how; the real scope of DOJ's county letters (18 to all 58) is unresolved, as is which conflicting birthplace statistic (25.8% vs. 38.9%) is accurate, and how DOJ's list was actually compiled [F7][F12][F14].
review.whats_new: A Ninth Circuit panel heard a rare Sunday oral argument on DOJ's bid to block roughly 20,000 California mail ballots; two of three judges voiced skepticism about DOJ's authority and its list [F1][F2][F3]. The panel took the case under submission, with no ruling yet [F7].
review.local_opinions: The administration and allied Republicans argue DOJ's count is only a floor, and that counting disputed ballots before verification permanently dilutes citizens' votes [L1]. California election officials and county attorneys counter that DOJ's list is unverified and that segregating ballots now would itself disenfranchise eligible voters [L2]. Voting-rights groups and Congressional Democrats call the effort suppression, not fraud enforcement [L3]. After the Oct. 25 hearing, two judges, including a Trump appointee, doubted both DOJ's jurisdiction and its list, weakening L1's footing while echoing L2's own arguments; no reaction from L3 was found [L1][L2][L3].
review.world_opinions: International liberal outlets like Al Jazeera and The Guardian frame the fight as one more episode of Trump-era democratic backsliding, largely skipping the Elections Clause/federalism argument that drives the U.S. debate between L1 and L2/L3 [W1]. Canadian outlets CBC and The Globe and Mail instead treat the same enforcement sweep as a bilateral diplomatic incident, since Canadians are among those charged, and cover U.S.-Canada friction that none of L1, L2, or L3 raise [W2]. Only Al Jazeera's coverage reflects the Oct. 25 hearing itself; the Guardian, CBC and Globe and Mail pieces predate it [W1][W2].

timeline.event: DOJ sends LA County Registrar Dean Logan a letter and USB drive with a list of ~20,000 people it believes are likely noncitizens who received CA mail ballots, demanding review and ballot segregation by Oct 15 at noon EST.
LA County publicly states it has not accessed the USB drive, citing security/privacy protocols.

CA Secretary of State Weber replies to DOJ, calling the 48-hour deadline unreasonable given ballots are already out; DOJ files its civil complaint against California, Weber, and Logan (No. 2:26-cv-12025).
DOJ announces 'Operation Protect the Vote,' charging 28 lawful permanent residents tied to the list with election-related federal felonies.
LA County files its opposition brief to DOJ's TRO application, disputing the reliability of DOJ's list with sample statistics.

DOJ escalates, sending letters to a disputed number of CA counties (reported variously as 57 of 58, at least 18, or every county) demanding identification and segregation of suspected-noncitizen ballots; DOJ also files an emergency request at the Ninth Circuit after the district judge had not ruled by DOJ's requested deadline.

Ninth Circuit panel (Bennett, Bumatay, Sanchez) holds a rare weekend, nearly two-hour videoconference oral argument in case No. 26-7070 on DOJ's bid for an injunction pending appeal; panel is skeptical of DOJ's jurisdictional and merits arguments, takes the case under submission without ruling.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter is scheduled to hold a hearing in Santa Ana on DOJ's request for a temporary restraining order; the Ninth Circuit has indicated it hopes to rule before then.

unknowns: Whether the Ninth Circuit panel will rule before Judge Carter's Oct. 27 district court hearing, and which way it will rule given the panel's stated skepticism of DOJ's jurisdictional and merits arguments.

What Judge Carter will decide at the Oct. 27 TRO hearing, and whether the Ninth Circuit's preemptive appeal has stripped him of authority to act in the meantime (a question Judge Bennett raised repeatedly but did not resolve).
The true scope of DOJ's Oct. 23-24 letter round (57 of 58 counties vs. at least 18 vs. every county) has not been reconciled by any outlet or by DOJ itself.

Which of the two conflicting birthplace-statistic figures (25.8% in the Flores declaration vs. 38.9% reported by ABC7, attributed to a Bhullar declaration) is accurate, or whether they measure different things -- the underlying sworn declarations were not available to check.

The ultimate reliability of DOJ's purchased noncitizen list: at the Ninth Circuit hearing, DOJ's own attorney could not tell the judges how the list was compiled or name the third-party sources used to build it.

Whether any of the 28 lawful permanent residents charged on Oct. 19 are connected to the ~20,000-name list currently in dispute, beyond DOJ's framing of the arrests as part of the same enforcement push.

Only Al Jazeera's world-press coverage reflects the Oct. 25 hearing itself; the Guardian, CBC and Globe and Mail pieces used here predate it, so how those outlets' audiences see the hearing's actual outcome is not known.

local_groups.label: Trump administration and allied Republicans: ballots should be set aside until citizenship is verified
local_groups.position: The Justice Department, under Attorney General Todd Blanche and led locally by First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, argues that federal data-matching has identified more than 20,000 people on California's rolls as likely noncitizens who were mailed 2026 ballots, and that letting those ballots be counted before citizenship is verified permanently dilutes the votes of eligible citizens. They present the emergency appeal to the Ninth Circuit as a narrow, urgent request to segregate (not cancel) disputed ballots, not an attack on anyone's right to vote.
arguments: DOJ says its own count is "a minimum of 20,000" likely noncitizens who received mail ballots this cycle, calling that figure "the floor," with a potentially much larger total.

Because processed mail ballots cannot later be traced back to the individual voter, the department argues every day of counting without segregation causes untraceable disenfranchisement and dilution of citizens' votes that cannot be undone afterward.
DOJ's attorney told the Ninth Circuit that California "isn't interested in enforcing" the state and federal bars on noncitizen voting, so the courts must act because the state will not.
local_groups.share_basis: Pew Research Center poll, fieldwork Sept. 28-Oct. 4, 2026: only 45% of voters backing Republican congressional candidates are confident noncitizens would be stopped if they tried to vote, versus 90% of Democratic-backing voters — pointing to a large bloc of Republican-aligned opinion receptive to stricter verification.
local_groups.on_development: At the Oct. 25 hearing, two of three judges -- including a Trump appointee -- voiced open skepticism on both jurisdiction and the reliability of DOJ's list, and DOJ's own attorney could not explain how the list was compiled or verified. The group's underlying demand (segregate the ballots) is unchanged, but its legal footing visibly weakened; no ruling had been issued as of the hearing.

representatives.quote: the problem is that California isn't interested in enforcing that provision
representatives.author: Matthew Donnelly, Justice Department attorney, quoted by the Los Angeles Times

representatives.quote: We believe it's at a minimum of 20,000. That's the floor.
representatives.author: Bill Essayli, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California

local_groups.label: California election officials and the state's courtroom attorneys: the federal list is unverified and the demand is unlawful
local_groups.position: California's Secretary of State, the Los Angeles County Registrar and the attorneys representing them in court argue DOJ has not shown reliable evidence that the flagged voters are actually noncitizens, that the Constitution's Elections Clause leaves ballot administration to the states, and that sequestering roughly 20,000 ballots in the final days before the Nov. 3 count would itself disenfranchise eligible voters based on an unverified list.
arguments: California's deputy solicitor general told the Ninth Circuit that DOJ's request "would sow confusion and risk disenfranchising voters, and it has no basis in law or in fact."

Los Angeles County's attorney argued that blocking the ballots is unnecessary because existing challenge procedures already let the government pursue individual noncitizen-voting prosecutions, and that segregating the ballots would do nothing to "prevent or impair in any way the government's ability to prosecute people for this federal misdemeanor."

State officials say DOJ has repeatedly changed its noncitizen estimates without disclosing its methodology, and that its "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data" only sow distrust in the election.
local_groups.share_basis: no direct poll of California officials' views found; assessed by prominence and breadth of officials and attorneys taking this position in court filings and coverage
local_groups.on_development: The group's position was echoed rather than shifted by the hearing: two of three Ninth Circuit judges, including a Trump appointee, questioned both DOJ's jurisdiction to appeal before the district court ruled and the reliability of its noncitizen list -- arguments California's own attorneys had already been making in their briefs. No ruling yet.

representatives.quote: Its request would sow confusion and risk disenfranchising voters, and it has no basis in law or in fact.
representatives.author: Samuel Siegel, California Deputy Solicitor General, in oral argument

representatives.quote: nothing about this process that will prevent or impair in any way the government's ability to prosecute people for this federal misdemeanor
representatives.author: Seth Waxman, attorney for LA County Registrar Dean Logan, in oral argument

representatives.quote: The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections.
representatives.author: Shirley N. Weber, California Secretary of State

local_groups.label: Voting-rights groups and Congressional Democrats: this is intimidation and suppression of voters, not integrity enforcement
local_groups.position: The NAACP, LULAC, the Campaign Legal Center, the Democracy Defenders Fund and Democratic members of Congress argue DOJ's lists of "likely noncitizens" rest on undisclosed, unreliable methodology, and that pursuing emergency court orders to block ballots while voting is already underway amounts to voter suppression and intimidation rather than a genuine fraud investigation.
arguments: The coalition that moved to intervene in the underlying case argues DOJ is "spreading misinformation" and "relying on faulty and unreliable data to disenfranchise voters," not responding to a real problem with the state's elections.
The NAACP calls the litigation part of "this administration's ongoing voter suppression campaign" and says it will "swiftly move to safeguard the right to vote."
LULAC argues DOJ "wants California to set aside ballots without establishing whether those people are actually eligible to vote," shifting the burden of proof onto voters rather than the government.
local_groups.share_basis: Pew Research Center poll, fieldwork Sept. 28-Oct. 4, 2026: 90% of voters backing Democratic congressional candidates say they are confident noncitizens would be stopped if they tried to vote, reflecting broad confidence among Democratic-aligned voters that existing safeguards work and skepticism that a new federal campaign is needed.

representatives.quote: The NAACP remains vigilant and will swiftly move to safeguard the right to vote in the face of this administration's ongoing voter suppression campaign.
representatives.author: Kristen Clarke, NAACP General Counsel

world_clusters.label: International press: ballot fight as the latest episode of Trump-era democratic backsliding
world_clusters.position: The Qatar-backed, state-funded broadcaster Al Jazeera and the UK's privately owned Guardian treat the roughly-20,000-ballot dispute less as a states'-rights legal puzzle than as the latest episode in a recurring pattern: a Justice Department using an undisclosed-methodology list and a compressed pre-election deadline to pressure state election machinery, after a documented false alarm over noncitizen voters in Nevada. Both outlets foreground DOJ officials' own admissions that the list likely includes citizens, and present Governor Newsom's and Secretary Weber's objections as the credible account; Al Jazeera's own copy explicitly labels the administration 'right-wing', a framing US domestic wire coverage avoids.
world_clusters.on_development: Al Jazeera published same-day, UTC-dated Oct 26 coverage of the Ninth Circuit hearing describing the panel as 'sceptical' and quoting Judge Bennett's Elections Clause objection to DOJ's request. The Guardian's dedicated piece on the list's reliability predates the hearing (Oct 20); no Guardian follow-up on the Oct 25 argument itself was found — no reaction found from the Guardian specifically on this development.

representatives.quote: Just because an alien says on a form that they are a citizen doesn't make them eligible to vote.
representatives.author: Kiersten Pels, Justice Department spokesperson, quoted by The Guardian

representatives.quote: This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day.
representatives.author: Gavin Newsom, California Governor, quoted by Al Jazeera

representatives.quote: The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting.
representatives.author: Al Jazeera (unsigned)

world_clusters.contrast_with_local: W1 overlaps substantively with L2's and L3's positions -- both question the reliability of DOJ's list and, in L3's case, call the campaign suppression -- but international coverage frames it as part of a global pattern of Trump-era democratic backsliding rather than, as the US domestic debate between L1 and L2 does, a states'-rights dispute over the Constitution's Elections Clause and federal-state authority over elections. L1's framing of the suit as a narrow, good-faith fraud-prevention measure is not engaged with at all in this coverage.

world_clusters.label: Canadian press: the enforcement campaign as a diplomatic incident, not a ballot-law dispute
world_clusters.position: CBC News and the privately owned Globe and Mail cover the noncitizen-voting crackdown primarily as a Canada-US friction story: at least 11-15 Canadians have been arrested or charged as part of the same 'Operation Protect the Vote' sweep that produced the California arrests tied to the DOJ's 20,000-name list, and the US Embassy in Ottawa has publicly accused Canadian politicians of 'openly attempting to influence the U.S. election through trade policy, political campaigning and public remarks', further claiming Canada has the second-highest number of its citizens facing illegal-voting charges of any country. Canadian officials, including Prime Minister Mark Carney and Industry Minister Melanie Joly, have rejected the interference accusation.
world_clusters.on_development: Both outlets' coverage runs Oct 21-23, before the Oct 25 Ninth Circuit hearing; no CBC or Globe and Mail follow-up tying the embassy dispute to the appeals-court argument was found — no reaction found on this specific development.

representatives.quote: All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections.
representatives.author: U.S. Embassy in Ottawa, quoted by CBC News
Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada, quoted by The Globe and Mail
Pete Hoekstra, U.S. Ambassador to Canada, quoted by The Globe and Mail

world_clusters.contrast_with_local: Inside the US the dispute is argued entirely between L1 (the administration) and L2/L3 (state officials and voting-rights groups) over election authority and the accuracy of DOJ's list; Canadian coverage barely engages that framing and instead treats the same enforcement sweep as a bilateral diplomatic incident -- evidence the 'likely noncitizen' list and prosecutions are landing on citizens of an allied country -- a dimension none of L1, L2, or L3 raise.
